title: 31st sitting of the 20th Majlis
presiding: Deputy Speaker Ahmed Nazim (as named in the minutes)
summary: The sitting opened with 42 members present. Members spent most of the morning in the initial debate on a bill to amend the Criminal Procedure Act so that police could have bank accounts or funds held in scam cases before a court order arrives. Nearly all speakers backed the aim; several said it would not stop scams by itself and that banking-law changes, bank safeguards and public awareness were also needed. After the sponsor closed the debate, the vote was left to the day's voting time, and members began continuing the debate on the government's Urban Development Bill, which was still open when this part ended. This part continues the debate on whether to accept the government's Urban Development Bill, which would let the state designate metropolitan areas, urban regions and urban centres. Government-side members said it would plan growth and spread services more fairly, while several MDP members questioned the broad powers it gives, its effect on local councils, and whether it would improve life on the islands. After a recess the Majlis voted to accept a Criminal Procedure Act amendment bill (72-0) and the Urban Development Bill (61-11-1), and sent both to committee. The text is partly garbled, so some speaker summaries are approximate.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Hussain
positions: On scams, said accounts are drained within about 45 minutes and asked why banks cannot temporarily block them; noted an anti-scam centre is being set up.
On the Urban Development Bill, supported it and argued Maldives needs a master plan and clear urban development rules, including options such as residency visas for investors.

speakers.name: Abdul Gafoor Moosa
positions: Says planning only matters if it brings residents services, income and hope, and sees little of that so far.
Says laws should deliver results for people, not headlines.

speakers.name: Mohamed Ibrahim
positions: Introduced the bill, saying scam victims lose money while a court order is awaited and police need a legal way to hold funds.
In closing, thanked members and urged a fast legal remedy given the number of scam reports.

speakers.name: Abdulla Rifau
positions: Supported the bill but warned that freezing a whole account could harm innocent businesses; suggested blocking only the suspected amount.
On the Urban Development Bill, thanked the sponsor and noted the manifesto promise of development zones in the north and south.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Nazil
positions: Supported the amendment and noted the same matter is covered by a criminal procedure bill already in committee.
On the Urban Development Bill, thanked the sponsor and argued Malé land and flat allocations followed plans rather than political aims.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Didi
positions: Said many citizens lose money from accounts and that police told the committee they need a legal power to hold accounts during investigations.
Supports the bill; says larger planned urban areas let the state deliver constitutional basic services more fairly and cheaply, and hopes committee work is finished quickly.

speakers.name: Hassan Zareer
positions: Called the amendment good but raised concern about light court penalties compared with sums stolen.
On the Urban Development Bill, said Maldives still has no urban development law and pointed to Singapore and Malaysia as examples.

speakers.name: Hussain Shareef
positions: Asked whether the amendment would actually stop scams, pointing to fast account-to-account transfers and suggesting study of the banking system first.
Supports the bill as part of the President's long-term vision for planned development.
Says earlier Hulhumale' housing lacked services, and wants master plans protected so they cannot easily be undone.

speakers.name: Hussain Ziyad
positions: Supported the amendment overall; said police face obstacles, the banking system needs updating and public awareness is needed.
Argues that in nine months island services and projects have not progressed, and questions whether a new law will change that.

speakers.name: Qasim Ibrahim
positions: Supported it generally but said it will not stop scams; wants banking-law changes and banks to take responsibility for customers' money.
Supports the bill; calls for facing facts on national debt and for the government and Majlis to cooperate and cut spending.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Falah
positions: Said the amendment is not a bad one and that government is preparing amendments to several laws; stressed implementers must act honestly.
Raised a point of order that members were speaking about matters beyond the bill under debate.

speakers.name: Mohamed Abbas
positions: Fully supported the amendment, citing pensioners' and families' money being moved; wants the committee to consult banks and police.

speakers.name: Mauroof Zakir
positions: Supported the amendment, said scams are real and that members should protect citizens and refine the bill in committee.

speakers.name: Dr. Anara Naeem
positions: Backed the amendment in principle, stressing protection of property and that police must use their powers honestly.

speakers.name: Saudulla Hilmy
positions: Called the amendment important because police asked for it, and said victims need a chance to recover funds before they are moved on.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Muhammad
positions: Supported the bill and suggested people who knowingly join such schemes out of greed should face some penalty.

speakers.name: Ahmed Azaan Marzooq
positions: Said the amendment alone would not solve the problem; argued banking-law changes and rules to hold suspicious transfers are needed.

speakers.name: Husnee Mubarik
positions: Supported the intent but doubted amending section 73 would achieve it; said section 72 monitoring orders already exist and the banking law is the main route.

speakers.name: Ahmed Zahir
positions: Cited Bank of Maldives figures of 1,657 cases and MVR 26 million, and called for a holistic approach including automatic detection of fund-flow patterns.

speakers.name: Ameen Faisal
positions: Supported the amendment, citing police and bank figures showing the scale of the problem, and urged a quick legal remedy.

speakers.name: Abdul Sattar Mohamed
positions: Spoke for the Urban Development Bill, saying government does not intend to seize land and rejecting opposition criticism of land allocation.

speakers.name: Hassan Mufeed Abdul Gadir
positions: Supported the Urban Development Bill, saying it gives legal footing for national development zones and urged it be passed.

speakers.name: Mohamed Fazeel
positions: Supports the bill but wants committee amendments making the law hard to change, for example needing a two-thirds vote over about 15 years.

speakers.name: Mohamed Alsan Ahmed
positions: Supports the bill; says unplanned migration to Male' caused hardship, and urges inclusive planning and quick passage after committee consultation.

speakers.name: Mohamed Mamdooh
positions: Backs the bill as the first law giving legal power to develop urban centres, regions and metropolitan areas, and criticises MDP-era island project delivery.

speakers.name: Ahmed Didi
positions: Questions the bill's purpose, saying regional offices move power toward central government.
Worries that the word 'city' or 'urban centre' could confuse tourists and hurt island marketing.

speakers.name: Dr. Ahmed Shamheed
positions: Concerned the bill is broadly worded, with unclear powers for the minister, urban unit and councils, and that local councils lose authority; hopes committee fixes this.

speakers.name: Ahmed Thariq
positions: Supports defining urban centres, saying the state must provide basic services, and links this to the need to manage debt and spending.

speakers.name: Azim Abdul Azeez
positions: As sponsor, says members showed the bill's importance, notes very small islands struggle to sustain services, and asks the committee to study and pass it quickly.

decisions: Initial debate on the Criminal Procedure Act amendment bill (Act 2016/12) ended; the vote was left to the day's voting time.
Debate on the Urban Development Bill continued and was still open at the end of this part.
Bill to amend the Criminal Procedure Act (Law 12/2016) accepted for consideration and sent to the Judiciary Committee.
Urban Development Bill accepted at first stage and sent to a joint committee of the National Development and Heritage and Decentralisation committees.
Next sitting announced for Thursday 22 August 2024.

votes.what: Accept the bill to amend the Criminal Procedure Act (Law 12/2016) for consideration
Accept the Urban Development Bill for consideration
